final_recommendation: The room converged on a detailed labor enforcement Protocol amendment framework (five triggers, Mexican-led joint inspections, automatic tariffs on joint findings, 14-day House vote timeline) but collapsed at the final stage when Mexico demanded consultation rights before tariff triggers, which the U.S. Congressman's caucus would interpret as a loophole. No consensus was reached on bridging Mexico's sovereignty red line with U.S. demands for truly automatic enforcement.
minority_objections: Mexico's government rejected pre-authorized automatic tariffs without consultation/interpretation rights, stating their Congress will not ratify a framework that 'cedes enforcement to a joint body we don't control'
Business lobby initially pushed for joint public statement before draft text was locked, contradicting the Congressman's demand to vote on text not promises
key_conflicts: Mexico's sovereignty concern (consultation rights before tariff triggers) vs. U.S. Congress demand for automatic enforcement with no re-litigation loophole
Timeline pressure (14-day House vote deadline) vs. need for Mexico's Congress to ratify tariff schedule before U.S. public announcement
Media/public narrative pressure to announce 'labor wins teeth' vs. risk of premature announcement before text gaps are closed
key_concessions: U.S. accepted Mexican inspectors leading every joint team (not unilateral U.S. inspections)
Mexico accepted joint findings triggering consequences (not unilateral Mexican veto)
Business lobby accepted 60-day amendment timeline cap with inspection/tariff mechanisms
Canada secured explicit carve-out: labor protocol amendments standalone, no reopening of Chapter 19 or dairy
All parties converged on five specific violation triggers (organizing, wage audits, forced labor, child labor, safety) rather than open-ended enforcement
red_lines: U.S. Congressman: tariffs must be automatic on joint findings with zero re-vote or re-litigation by Mexico
Mexico: will not ratify framework that eliminates their Congress's interpretation rights over joint findings
Labor union: 48-hour unannounced access and automatic tariffs or public blocking campaign
Canada: labor amendments must not reopen Chapter 19 or dairy concessions
Business lobby: 14-day House vote deadline to prevent deal slipping into January
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: The room did not seriously address what happens if Mexico's Congress rejects the tariff schedule after U.S. public commitment
No discussion of how to handle disputes over whether a 'joint finding' threshold was actually met
Limited attention to whether five triggers are sufficient to satisfy labor union membership vs. broader Democratic caucus concerns
Minimal exploration of Canadian domestic political risk if U.S.-Mexico enforcement disputes spill over into trilateral agreement stability
downstream_risk_variables: Mexico's Congress ratification vote timing and outcome on pre-authorized tariff schedule
Whether trade lawyer's 'rebuttal with evidence within 48 hours' language can bridge Mexico sovereignty concern and U.S. automaticity demand
U.S. Democratic caucus reaction to Wednesday draft text—whether five triggers and joint-team structure are sufficient
Media narrative control if Thursday announcement is delayed or if Mexico requests tweaks post-announcement
Business community confidence if 14-day timeline slips or if enforcement mechanism creates ongoing uncertainty
uncertainty_notes: The room built detailed enforcement architecture but failed to resolve the core tension: Mexico needs consultation/interpretation rights to defend sovereignty domestically, while U.S. Congress needs automatic consequences to prove enforcement is real. The trade lawyer's proposed 'rebuttal mechanism' was not tested for acceptability by either Mexico or the Congressman. It remains unclear whether any language can thread this needle, or whether one side must capitulate. The 14-day House vote deadline creates extreme time pressure that may force a choice between imperfect text and no deal.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Dominated the room: Congressman repeatedly stated caucus won't vote without locked text, Mexico's ratification sequencing became a blocking issue, and the final proposal collapsed because Mexico's sovereignty objection made ratification impossible under U.S. terms.
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Central driver: Five specific triggers, 48-hour inspection windows, automatic tariffs, and joint-team structure were negotiated in granular detail across all rounds. Union set red line that vague language kills enforcement, and this shaped every subsequent exchange.
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Genuinely discussed: Business lobby accepted Protocol amendment and set 14-day House vote deadline, but was not the dominant force—played supporting role to Congressional and labor demands rather than driving the room's direction.
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Mentioned and secured (carve-out on Chapter 19/dairy) but not a driving theme—Canada's concerns were addressed early and did not shape subsequent rounds focused on U.S.-Mexico enforcement mechanics.
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Central blocking issue: Mexico's demand for consultation rights before automatic tariffs drove the final collapse. Repeatedly stated Congress will not ratify framework that 'cedes enforcement to a joint body we don't control.' This red line could not be bridged.
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Developed consideration: Media actor repeatedly pressed on narrative control ('USMCA stalled' vs. 'labor wins teeth'), timing of announcements, and headline risk if enforcement appears weak. Shaped urgency but did not drive substantive positions.
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Discussed as contingent: Room treated ratification as requiring Protocol amendment to pass, and multiple exchanges addressed risk that Mexico's post-announcement tweaks or U.S. caucus rejection would destabilize the entire package. Not the dominant thread but a real concern.
